newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: COTTON - Rates seen down in India, mixed in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: COTTON - Rates seen down in India, mixed in Pakistan.

text.p: Indian cotton prices are expected to fall next week on higher new crop arrivals and sluggish demand from spinners while Pakistani rates are likely to remain mixed, dealers said on Thursday.
In India, dealers said more arrivals and slow mill demand pushed prices down. Reports that the government authorised exports of about 100,000 (170-kg) bales failed to give a boost.
Daily new crop arrivals of Bengal-deshi in northern states, where crops have matured well, were about 900/1,000 bales and were expected to increase in October, one trader said.
The new crop in northern India is expected to be 5.0 million bales against 4.0 million last year.
Cotton prices rose two weeks ago on reports that a viral disease had hit the northern crop, but fell when it became clear that the standing crop had not been affected, traders said.
In spot deals Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) fell to 13,200/13,500 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) from 14,000-14,200.
Bengal-deshi for ready delivery fell to 825-830 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) from 875-900 and lost 75-80 to 860-865 per maund for October delivery.

"Production of cotton in China, Turkey and Uzbekistan is projected lower and prospects are bright for export of Indian cotton," another trader said, adding that prices were unlikely to fall substantially due to the government's priority towards export and rising domestic consumption.
Pakistan's market direction was unclear. It ended mixed on Thursday after spinners bought heavily to capitalise on a drastic price fall in the past week, brokers said.

"Rates went up on technical grounds as spinners rushed to buy cotton following a sharp fall on higher arrivals of raw cotton at ginning factories," said broker Nasim Usman at the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA).
NIAB-78 variety rebounded to 2,343 rupees per maund on Thursday after falling to 2,288 on Wednesday from 2,618 on September 12, Usman said.
Spinners foresaw rates dropping on higher arrivals but dealers expected moderate rises on buying by exporters, he said.
The government has promised to maintain its free trade policy in cotton until June 1998.
ON the kerb, NIAB-78 fluctuated between 2,150 and 2,175 rupees on Thursday -- still seen as high for exporters.
"Exporters are likely to enter the market after the rates touch 1,900 per maund," Usman said.
The 1996/97 crop was likely to yield 11 million 375-lb bales but ginners expect a crop of about 12.5 million, he said.
